```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette shows how to build historical series of formal employment with
**datarais**, from the DuckDB tables to the charts. To keep the vignette fast
and runnable without internet access, it uses a **small synthetic table** with
the same columns as the real data. The numbers are random and meaningless; the
code is what you would run on the real database (see the last section).

## 1. The data

The RAIS tables are split by layout: `rais_antigo` holds the years up to 2017
and `rais_novo` the years from 2018. The synthetic database below mimics that
split.

```{r toy-data}
library(datarais)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(2024)
cnae <- c("01113", "10113", "29107", "41018", "47113",
          "62015", "84116", "85139", "86100")
ufs  <- c(23L, 24L, 29L, 35L)   # CE, RN, BA, SP (IBGE codes)

make_year <- function(y) {
  d <- expand.grid(ano = y, sigla_uf = ufs, cnae20_classe = cnae,
                   i = 1:6, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  d$i <- NULL
  d$vl_remun_media_nom <- round(runif(nrow(d), 1300, 6500) * (1 + 0.04 * (y - 2016)), 2)
  d
}

anos <- 2016:2019
db   <- tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb")
con  <- rais_connect(db, quiet = TRUE)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "rais_antigo", bind_rows(lapply(2016:2017, make_year)))
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "rais_novo",   bind_rows(lapply(2018:2019, make_year)))
```

A series that crosses 2018 is built year by year: `rais_tbl(con, year = y)`
chooses the right table and filters the year.

## 2. Series by state

In the RAIS tables, `sigla_uf` is the numeric IBGE code of the state. The
`uf_codigos` table translates it to the abbreviation and the region.

```{r serie-uf}
serie_uf <- purrr::map(anos, function(y) {
  rais_tbl(con, year = y) |>
    group_by(ano, sigla_uf) |>
    summarise(
      vinculos      = n(),
      salario_medio = mean(vl_remun_media_nom, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    collect()
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  left_join(uf_codigos, by = c("sigla_uf" = "codigo")) |>
  arrange(ano, sigla)

serie_uf
```

```{r plot-uf, eval=has_gg}
library(ggplot2)

serie_uf |>
  filter(regiao == "Nordeste") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ano, y = vinculos, colour = sigla)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = anos) +
  labs(
    title    = "Formal employment in the Northeast (synthetic data)",
    subtitle = "Number of job records per year",
    x = NULL, y = "Jobs", colour = "State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 3. Series by sector (CNAE 2.0)

The tables store the CNAE 2.0 class (5 digits). The division (2 digits) used
below is its first two digits. Sums and counts are computed in the database and
combined afterwards, so the average salary of a division is weighted by the
number of jobs.

```{r serie-setor}
setores <- tibble::tibble(
  divisao = c("01", "10", "29", "41", "47", "62", "84", "85", "86"),
  setor   = c("Agriculture", "Food products", "Motor vehicles",
              "Construction", "Retail trade", "IT services",
              "Public administration", "Education", "Health care")
)

por_classe <- purrr::map(anos, function(y) {
  rais_tbl(con, year = y) |>
    filter(!is.na(cnae20_classe)) |>
    group_by(ano, cnae20_classe) |>
    summarise(
      vinculos = n(),
      soma_rem = sum(vl_remun_media_nom, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_rem    = sum(ifelse(is.na(vl_remun_media_nom), 0, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) |>
    collect()
}) |>
  bind_rows()

serie_setor <- por_classe |>
  mutate(divisao = substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(cnae20_classe)), 1, 2)) |>
  inner_join(setores, by = "divisao") |>
  group_by(ano, setor) |>
  summarise(
    vinculos      = sum(vinculos),
    salario_medio = sum(soma_rem) / sum(n_rem),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

serie_setor |>
  filter(ano == max(ano)) |>
  arrange(desc(salario_medio))
```

```{r plot-setor, eval=has_gg}
serie_setor |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ano, y = salario_medio, colour = setor)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = anos) +
  labs(
    title    = "Average salary by sector (synthetic data)",
    x = NULL, y = "Average salary", colour = "Sector"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## 4. Average salary by state and sector

```{r heatmap, eval=has_gg}
ano_ref <- max(anos)

rais_tbl(con, year = ano_ref) |>
  filter(!is.na(cnae20_classe)) |>
  group_by(sigla_uf, cnae20_classe) |>
  summarise(
    soma_rem = sum(vl_remun_media_nom, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_rem    = sum(ifelse(is.na(vl_remun_media_nom), 0, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(uf_codigos, by = c("sigla_uf" = "codigo")) |>
  filter(regiao == "Nordeste") |>
  mutate(divisao = substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(cnae20_classe)), 1, 2)) |>
  inner_join(setores, by = "divisao") |>
  group_by(sigla, setor) |>
  summarise(salario = sum(soma_rem) / sum(n_rem), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = setor, y = sigla, fill = salario)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(salario)), size = 2.5, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  labs(
    title = paste("Average salary by sector and state,", ano_ref, "(synthetic data)"),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Average\nsalary"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
```

```{r cleanup}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
unlink(db)
```

## 5. Reading the results correctly

Before using these series in a study, keep in mind:

* **Nominal values.** `vl_remun_media_nom` is in current reais of each year.
  To compare years, deflate it (for example with the IPCA) before averaging
  across time.
* **State column.** `sigla_uf` holds the IBGE code, not the abbreviation. Join
  with `uf_codigos` as shown above.
* **CNAE availability.** `cnae20_classe` exists only from 2006. Series by sector
  that start earlier need the CNAE 1.0 variable (`cnae95_classe`) and a
  correspondence table.
* **Layout change in 2018.** Files up to 2017 are split by state and from 2018
  by region, with different variables. Check `rais_layouts()` and
  `rais_col_dictionary()` before comparing variables across the break.
* **Active jobs.** The tables contain job records, which are not the same as
  employed people. Filter the employment status variable if you need only jobs
  active on 31 December.

## 6. Running it on the real data

The code above works on the real database. Because the files are large, start
small. For the old layout (up to 2017) the files are split by state, so
`state` limits the download:

```{r real-small, eval=FALSE}
db <- "rais.duckdb"

# Two years, one state: a small download (layout up to 2017)
rais_load(years = 2016:2017, state = "RN", db_path = db)
con <- rais_connect(db)
```

From 2018 onwards `state` is ignored, because the files are distributed by
region: the whole region file is downloaded, and you filter the state after
loading, for example with `filter(sigla_uf == 24L)`.

For the full series, load all the years you need (this is a large download)
and reuse the code of the previous sections with `anos <- 2010:2023`:

```{r real-full, eval=FALSE}
options(
  datarais.cache_dir = tools::R_user_dir("datarais", "cache"),
  datarais.workers   = 3
)
rais_load(years = 2010:2023, type = "vinculos", db_path = db)
```

To share the result with Python, Spark or other tools, export to Parquet. Close
the connection first, because DuckDB does not allow a second connection to the
same file with a different configuration:

```{r parquet, eval=FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
rais_to_parquet(db, output_dir = "parquet", partition_by = "sigla_uf")
```
